prime.problem: The three cards answer three different questions about one run, and it's easy to blur them into one. A run can be single, durable and finished, and still be wrong: the Tuesday run was all three and ended with a false "all tests pass".
prime.fits: The map for course 1 of The Agent Stack: read it first to see the three owners, or last as a recap. It builds on the agent loop: the loop is what runs inside one turn, and this course is about who owns the run around it.
expect: three owners: control plane, runtime, verifier
done = R ∧ T ∧ C ∧ V ∧ D
levers grouped by what they change

must: Each owner answers a different question → the control plane decides which run and who may write, the runtime records which steps happened once, the verifier checks whether it worked → getting the first two right gives one clean run, not a correct one
done = R ∧ T ∧ C ∧ V ∧ D → any later link can be false while every earlier one holds → the final message is evidence of R only, so a false success claim is S ∧ ¬V

A compaction summary is written over the raw tool results → it can upgrade exit 1 to "tests passing" → every later message repeats it → only a verifier that re-runs the check outside the agent catches it

compress.prompt: Card closed. Draw the mental model: the five boxes of the top row (events, control plane, runtime, world, verifier) and the five claim-chain links underneath, each with its owner. Then write both formulas and fill in the Tuesday run's values.
checklist: control plane owns the session, runtime owns progress, verifier owns the evidence
links: request, tool, command, effect verified, delivered, each with its own owner
done = R ∧ T ∧ C ∧ V ∧ D = 1 ∧ 1 ∧ 0 ∧ 0 ∧ 1 = 0 for the Tuesday run
the claim entered at the step-7 compaction summary, not at step 9

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between a run being single, durable and done, and name the owner responsible for each.
answer: single: one run writes the session, duplicates dropped (control plane)
durable: each step recorded, so a crash neither repeats effects nor loses waits (runtime)
done: every link of the chain holds, checked from outside (verifier)
the first two don't imply the third

retrieve.q: Walk through the Tuesday run's formula: give each of R, T, C, V, D and S its value with the evidence that sets it, then compute done and the false-claim value.
answer: R = 1: the loop returned a final message at step 9
T = 1: the pytest call returned a result
C = 0: that result was exit code 1
V = 0: the checker's re-run also exited 1
D = 1: the message reached the user; S = 1: it says all tests pass

retrieve.q: You have one week on a harness that pushes branches and reports success. Which lever from the ranking do you build first, and what risk do you accept by deferring the rest?
answer: an outside verifier first: it is the only lever that catches a false claim
then an idempotency key on the push, the cheapest guard against a duplicate effect
deferring the journal accepts rework after a crash (14.10 vs 7.50 steps per run in the simulation)
deferring the busy policy accepts late corrections

compare.q: The basics overview's formula counts input tokens (N × P + Δ × N(N − 1) ÷ 2); this one is a logical AND. What does each measure, and what would each miss about the Tuesday run?
answer: the token formula measures cost and size; it is the same whether pytest passed or failed
this formula measures whether the run worked; it says nothing about cost
both put the fix in the harness rather than the model
a cheap run can be wrong and an expensive one right, so you need both views

predict.q: A different run: the agent edits test_parse_due_date so it passes, pytest exits 0, and the checker re-runs the same edited tests and exits 0. Commit to values for C, V and the false-claim result, then say what the formula misses.
predict.answer: By the formula C = 1, V = 1, so done = 1 and the false-claim value is 0. But the effect wasn't verified: the verifier checked the agent's own edited tests. The done-chain card's caption says a real checker re-runs tests it will accept and checks the tests weren't edited. V is only as good as the verifier's independence.

apply.task: Take a recent run of an agent you use that ended with a success message. Fill in R, T, C, V, D and S from its transcript plus one re-run of its tests, name the owner that recorded each value, and compute done and the false-claim value.
apply.done: You have six values, each with a piece of evidence (a message, a tool record, an exit code, your re-run) and an owner, and the two results.
apply.hint: If the transcript was compacted, check the summary's wording against the raw tool result it replaced.
